review.scope: Focused shared intake on post-election statements, Iran mediation, Nvidia’s inquiry and Israel’s mandate ceremony. Remaining election calls, court dispositions, the Miller handover and operational military decisions remain incompletely verified. All other issue findings are carried.

administration.headline: Trump offers room for policy talks while his advisers prepare to resist congressional investigations.
administration.summary: Trump retains executive authority after Republicans lost the midterms, while Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January. His post-election interview permits Vice President JD Vance to criticize the Iran war and raises the possibility of an immigration agreement, but establishes no implemented policy reversal. Naming Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles could strengthen an advocate of stricter immigration enforcement; this review has not confirmed today’s operational handover or Wiles’s new responsibilities. Attorney General Todd Blanche is publicly preparing to defend officials against congressional investigations. Iran mediation offers Vance a chance to show results, but the planned Qatar meeting has not produced a verified agreement. Nvidia’s board has opened an inquiry that could strengthen demands for scrutiny of chip exports, without establishing a security breach or a new export restriction. Israel’s president has delivered a mandate to try forming a government to Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot; a new coalition is still unresolved. The Fed dispute, tariffs, Epstein oversight, immigration litigation, Venezuela and Russia retain consequential verification gaps. These limits prevent a claim that the administration has already changed course.

contests.title: Miller is set to replace Wiles as White House chief of staff
contests.assessment: As chief of staff, Miller would have more say over White House staffing and the proposals presented to Trump. Wiles is reported to be moving to Trump’s political team, where she may continue advising him about elections. Her new responsibilities, including any influence over campaign money, are not yet confirmed.
contests.authority: Trump chooses his chief of staff. The reported handover from Wiles to Miller is November 9.
contests.leverage: The chief of staff helps manage access to Trump and the work of senior White House staff. A role on Trump’s political team may still give Wiles influence, but does not give her the same daily control over White House work.
contests.change: Trump has announced the appointment. The review has not yet confirmed the handover or how the two advisers will divide their responsibilities.

basis.actions: Trump announced that Miller would replace Wiles as chief of staff.
basis.positions: Public congratulations show support for the appointment; they do not establish whom anyone will back for president in 2028.
basis.money: No evidence establishes that a payment caused the appointment. Wiles’s possible influence over campaign funds must be checked separately from her White House job.

contests.watch: The reported November 9 handover is due today. Confirm Miller’s actual responsibilities and Wiles’s political role; this intake did not establish operational completion.
contests.summary: Trump has named Stephen Miller to succeed Susie Wiles. The reported November 9 handover would put Miller in a stronger position to influence which officials and proposals reach Trump.

contests.title: Vance urges an end to the Iran war while Rubio defends Trump’s decision
contests.assessment: Vance can use negotiations and his criticism of the war to argue for a different approach. Rubio offers a competing argument for Trump’s original decision. Those arguments may shape Trump’s options and the nomination contest, but neither establishes that a settlement or another military operation has been approved.
contests.authority: Trump makes executive military decisions. Congress can authorize military action and decide funding; negotiations also require agreement from the other side.
contests.leverage: Officials negotiating with Iran can shape the terms presented to Trump. Advisers arguing for more military pressure can offer competing options. Public criticism can change who receives blame even before policy changes.
contests.change: Reuters reports a planned November 9 meeting with Qatar’s prime minister and continued disagreement over Iran’s terms. No completed meeting, accepted agreement or new US operational order was verified.

basis.actions: Trump reviewed options; Vance has led negotiations.
basis.positions: Vance publicly blamed the war for electoral losses; Rubio defended Trump’s decision.
basis.money: Deal-Capital’s business exposure is relevant context, not proof of donor direction of negotiations.

contests.watch: Verify the Qatar meeting’s outcome, the parties’ accepted terms and any military orders; distinguish Iranian strike reports from US confirmation.
contests.summary: Vance has argued that the war hurt Republicans in the election and has led negotiations. Rubio has defended Trump’s decision to use force. Trump still decides the next military step.

contests.title: Vance and his rivals compete for Trump’s voters, donors and campaign teams
contests.assessment: Vance’s Republican fundraising role and connections to donors and activist organizations could help him start a presidential campaign quickly. Rubio and other rivals have their own relationships and reasons to run. Public praise, donor interest and a formal endorsement are different levels of commitment.
contests.authority: Republican primary voters and convention delegates select the nominee. Trump can endorse a candidate and encourage his supporters to back that person, but he does not select the nominee on his own.
contests.leverage: Fundraisers can supply campaign money; activists can recruit volunteers; endorsements can help voters choose among candidates. A relationship helps only if the people involved actually commit support.
contests.change: In an interview recorded November 6 and published November 8, Trump acknowledged discussing Vance’s Iran post beforehand while emphasizing that Vance participated in decisions. This supports room for disagreement without demonstrating a break or new primary votes.

basis.actions: The RNC finance role, Malik fundraiser and Turning Point backing are concrete channels.
basis.positions: Public deferral, message support and a candidate endorsement mean different things.
basis.money: Thiel’s historical backing and Rockbridge access help explain Vance’s network; Griffin’s reported preference is not a Rubio contribution pledge.

contests.watch: Watch for announced campaigns, endorsements, committed funding, named organizers in early-primary states and voter surveys.
contests.summary: Vance has the strongest documented fundraising and activist connections among the tracked candidates. Rubio and other rivals could recruit some of the same supporters; Trump has not settled the race.

contests.title: Trump’s attempt to remove Lisa Cook faces legal challenges
contests.assessment: Trump’s effort to remove Cook could affect who serves on the Federal Reserve’s governing board. Courts and the required hearing process limit how that effort proceeds. Interest-rate decisions still belong to the Federal Open Market Committee, which includes Federal Reserve governors and regional bank presidents.
contests.authority: The Federal Open Market Committee votes on interest rates. The dispute over Cook’s removal involves the president, the courts and the procedures required by law.
contests.leverage: White House officials can press for a change in Fed leadership or lower rates. Treasury officials can advise on the market consequences, but neither group can simply order the committee to change its rate vote.
contests.change: The review records a delayed hearing and a later filing about the process. It has not confirmed a completed removal or a changed rate decision.

basis.actions: The hearing was delayed; the later filing addressed scheduling and participation.
basis.positions: Calls for lower rates do not establish a changed vote or removal.
basis.money: Market exposure can explain interests; no payment causing a rate decision is established.

contests.watch: Check the hearing date, court orders, any final removal decision and the committee’s actual rate votes.
contests.summary: The dispute over Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook’s position remains subject to court and hearing procedures. White House demands for lower rates do not give advisers the authority to set them.

contests.title: Justice Department departures could give Blanche more control over senior appointments
contests.summary: Reported departures leave Attorney General Todd Blanche with opportunities to replace senior managers. New managers could continue the same cases rather than signal a retreat from them.
contests.assessment: Replacing senior Justice Department officials can change who supervises cases and where staff and resources are assigned. Blanche could gain more control over those choices. Departures alone do not establish that a case has ended or that the administration has changed its enforcement policy. Blanche’s November 8 public defense of officials signals resistance to incoming investigations, but does not prove that records will be withheld lawfully or that an investigation will be stopped.
contests.authority: The attorney general directs the Justice Department. Different jobs may require presidential appointment, Senate confirmation or a temporary acting appointment.
contests.leverage: Department leaders can choose or propose replacements, assign supervisors and shift resources between cases. Those choices matter more than an announcement of departures on its own.
contests.change: Three leadership departures were reported. Their replacements and any resulting changes to investigations remain unverified.

basis.actions: CNN reported the named leadership departures on November 6.
basis.positions: The departures do not by themselves establish a public reversal of Justice Department policy.
basis.money: The reviewed reporting does not establish that money caused the departures. Possible career incentives are an interpretation, not a documented explanation from the officials.

contests.watch: Identify the replacements, confirm who is acting in each job and check whether cases, staffing or written instructions actually change.

nomination.headline: Vance leads, but rivals could win Republicans unhappy with Trump’s record.
nomination.summary: Vance leads because existing fundraising and activist relationships can help him organize while rivals compete for overlapping supporters. Policy disagreement alone does not make a rival a preferred president. DeSantis and Kemp can offer governing experience outside Washington; Paul and Massie must broaden support beyond liberty activists. McEntee could use media and personnel contacts to build a campaign, but attention is not a commitment to vote or volunteer. These are conditional forecasts, with most present support relationships still incompletely measured. Trump’s acknowledgment that Vance discussed his Iran criticism with him strengthens the case that Vance can seek correction without an immediate personal rupture. Whether voters regard that as leadership or shifting blame remains unmeasured. Daily estimates remain those of the November 8 full review.

candidates.path: Vance would claim credit for negotiations and offer corrections while trying to retain Trump’s support. He can recruit early-state staff through existing political relationships; disappointed activists can still defect.
candidates.coalition: Vance could retain Trump-aligned voters who want tighter immigration rules and relief from war and household costs. Existing Republican fundraising and activist relationships could help recruit staff and volunteers, but an introduction or endorsement does not guarantee votes.
candidates.advantage: Trump’s acknowledgment of their prior discussion gives Vance room to argue for correction while retaining access to the president. Talks with Qatar offer a chance to demonstrate results, if they produce an agreement.
candidates.vulnerability: Trump also emphasizes Vance’s role in decisions. Permission to criticize cannot erase responsibility or establish that voters trust the change.
candidates.positions: Vance favors tighter immigration rules and economic policies presented as helping American workers and families. He has also argued for negotiations over Iran; that does not erase his earlier public support for administration decisions.
candidates.money: Peter Thiel previously financed Vance’s political rise. Rockbridge and other Republican fundraising relationships could help a campaign, but past support does not establish a new 2028 commitment.

candidates.path: Rubio would defend his foreign-policy judgment and decide whether to seek an independent mandate rather than support Vance. Former campaign and official contacts could recruit staff; current office does not supply a presidential delegate team.
candidates.coalition: Rubio could recruit Republicans who favor a forceful foreign policy and donors who want an experienced official. Ken Griffin’s reported preference offers a possible fundraising opening, not a contribution pledge. Rubio would compete with Vance and Cruz for some of the same people.
candidates.advantage: His family narrative and conversational humor can make a national-security argument approachable. A reported warning about Nvidia gives him a possible national-security contrast, but the classified account and any voter response remain unverified.
candidates.vulnerability: Serving Trump while deferring on a bid can make him seem unwilling to lead independently.
candidates.positions: Rubio has defended Trump’s decision to use force against Iran. He could argue that pressure on U.S. adversaries is necessary, but voters may judge him by the war’s costs and results.
candidates.money: Some donors have expressed interest in Rubio. A reported preference is not the same as a pledge to finance his presidential campaign.

candidates.path: DeSantis would contrast Florida governance with federal failures and try to rebuild a more disciplined presidential team. A rebuilt national team could combine former staff with defectors; the 2024 campaign is experience rather than a ready-made operation.
candidates.coalition: DeSantis could recruit social conservatives and Republicans seeking an experienced governor. Former campaign staff and donors offer a starting point for rebuilding, but they can choose Kemp or another rival instead.
candidates.advantage: He can present a record of carrying out conservative policies as evidence that he would act decisively.
candidates.vulnerability: His previous campaign suggests difficulty turning policy approval into enough votes, though Trump’s hold on Republicans was another major obstacle.
candidates.positions: His record includes conservative policies enacted in Florida. His support for limited military strikes means that distance from the White House does not necessarily mean opposition to intervention abroad.
candidates.money: DeSantis has raised substantial money for past campaigns. That shows fundraising experience, but does not establish which donors would back another presidential bid.

candidates.path: Cruz would combine conservative credentials with criticism of economic decisions and seek an opening against Vance and Rubio. He could reactivate old organizers and recruit new ones, provided they choose this race over rival campaigns.
candidates.coalition: Cruz could recruit religious conservatives and activists who value a forceful ideological advocate. Past presidential organizers and donor relationships could help him start, but renewed commitments are uncertain and Rubio competes for security-minded supporters.
candidates.advantage: His detailed, combative arguments can signal conviction and preparation to conservative activists.
candidates.vulnerability: Voters tired of partisan combat may see the same style as rigid, while shifts toward Trump invite trust attacks.
candidates.positions: Cruz generally favors a forceful foreign policy but has criticized tariffs. These positions may attract different groups of Republican voters rather than one united base.
candidates.money: Donors supported Cruz in earlier presidential contests. We have not established that those relationships will become financial commitments for 2028.

candidates.path: McEntee could distinguish first-term personnel and withdrawal work from present federal decisions, while defending his Project 2025 work recruiting prospective officials for a later administration. Recruitment experience could help hire election specialists if willing supporters emerge; transition staffing is not delegate organizing.
candidates.coalition: McEntee could seek culturally conservative Trump supporters who want first-term policies with a different leader. His media audience could introduce him to potential supporters, while former personnel contacts might help recruit campaign specialists. Neither shows that people will donate, volunteer or vote for him.
candidates.advantage: Informal political communication could make an unfamiliar candidate approachable to some conservative viewers.
candidates.vulnerability: Attention to short-form content does not show that viewers trust him to govern or will work for a campaign.
candidates.positions: His first-term record includes support for restrictive immigration staffing and troop withdrawals. That record does not establish every position he would take in a presidential campaign today.
candidates.money: Technology investor Peter Thiel invested in McEntee’s dating business. That was a business investment, not a confirmed presidential-campaign contribution or endorsement.

candidates.path: Paul would make a case for limits on war and spending while trying to keep voters who still support much of Trump’s agenda. Political contacts can recruit organizers beyond Kentucky if interest broadens; cooperation with Massie does not guarantee a presidential endorsement.
candidates.coalition: Paul could recruit Republicans who want limits on spending and presidential war powers. His support for Massie shows cooperation despite Trump’s opposition, but a presidential contest could divide their overlapping activists and donors.
candidates.advantage: He can argue that constitutional limits deserve loyalty even when Trump disagrees.
candidates.vulnerability: Voters seeking immediate economic protection may resist his spending agenda or see him as too narrowly focused.
candidates.positions: Paul advocates limits on executive power, lower federal spending and freer trade. The review has not established all the immigration policies he would propose in a new presidential campaign.
candidates.money: Paul has historical links to the Protect Freedom political group and donor Jeff Yass. Those connections do not establish a confirmed financial commitment to a 2028 presidential bid.

candidates.path: Kemp would emphasize governing results and independence from federal decisions while deciding whether to pursue a national race. Georgia allies could recruit early-state specialists if he enters and attracts national demand.
candidates.coalition: Kemp’s Georgia supporters and state political relationships offer a base from which to recruit outside the state. Republicans looking for a governor could also choose DeSantis; Georgia approval does not establish national presidential preference.
candidates.advantage: He can use concrete governing examples and personal experience to make a restrained executive pitch.
candidates.vulnerability: A strong state reputation may leave national voters unmoved, and Trump loyalists may question him.
candidates.positions: His Georgia record includes tax cuts and conservative immigration, policing and social policies. A state record does not establish a complete presidential platform.
candidates.money: This review has not verified commitments from donors to finance a Kemp presidential campaign.

candidates.path: Massie would press accountability and war-powers claims and must choose whether a presidential effort would stay inside the Republican Party. Activists could recruit state specialists if he chooses a Republican campaign; oversight publicity alone will not qualify delegates.
candidates.coalition: Massie could recruit Republicans who value his challenges to presidential war-making and his oversight efforts. Past House-race fundraising shows some willingness to act, but Paul competes for overlapping supporters and Massie has not settled on a Republican presidential campaign.
candidates.advantage: He can point to opposition taken under pressure as evidence that he means what he says.
candidates.vulnerability: Admiring dissent does not mean wanting him as president, and a non-Republican route cannot win this nomination.
candidates.positions: Massie has pushed for congressional approval of military action and disclosure of government records. The review has not established a complete current presidential platform.
candidates.money: Groups spent money supporting Massie in his House primary. That does not establish that he controls those funds or that the same groups would finance a presidential campaign.

recovery.title: Peace and lower household costs restore Republican confidence in Trump’s allies
recovery.summary: War conditions and household costs improve enough that Republican voters regain confidence in Trump’s allies. Later disclosures do not undo that recovery.

managed_costs.title: Republicans remain dissatisfied, but Trump’s allies keep voters and campaign teams
managed_costs.summary: Republican voters remain unhappy with costs and policy results, but neither investigations nor a rival campaign persuades enough of them to abandon Trump’s allies. Existing campaign relationships help those allies remain competitive.

systemic.title: Republican voters blame senior Trump officials and seek a different leader
systemic.summary: Continuing policy failures or credible disclosures persuade a consequential group of Republican voters to blame senior Trump officials. Those voters reject an explanation that blames only subordinates and look for different leadership.

selective.title: Republicans blame particular officials while accepting a successor’s corrections
selective.summary: Republican voters accept that particular officials deserve blame while a successor offers a believable correction. They neither forgive the whole administration’s record nor reject all its senior allies.

backlash.title: Republicans rally behind Trump’s allies against Democratic investigations
backlash.summary: Democratic investigations fail to persuade enough Republican voters. Conflict with Democrats becomes a stronger reason to support Trump’s allies, even though policy results have not substantially improved.

cross_implications.title: Vance’s war criticism could help him compete with Rubio.
cross_implications.assessment: Vance can argue that he wants to end a war Rubio has defended. Rivals can also point to Vance’s earlier public defenses of the administration and question when he changed his position. The statement alone does not show which candidate voters now prefer.

cross_implications.title: Miller could shape which advisers and proposals reach Trump.
cross_implications.assessment: If Miller takes over as chief of staff, candidates seeking Trump’s help may have to work with him and his staff. The appointment does not establish that Miller or Trump has endorsed a 2028 candidate.

cross_implications.title: Justice Department departures could strengthen Blanche while Miller gains a White House role.
cross_implications.assessment: Blanche may be able to choose replacements and direct managers after the reported departures. Miller’s prospective White House role gives him a different way to influence decisions. Neither change alone proves that investigations will stop or policy will change.

cross_implications.title: Trump permits Vance’s Iran criticism while keeping him tied to administration decisions.
cross_implications.assessment: The prior discussion preserves Vance’s relationship with Trump while he argues for a different course. Negotiations could strengthen that argument if they deliver results; the planned Qatar meeting has not established an agreement or electoral gain.

relationships.kind: Different positions on the Iran war
relationships.assessment: Vance’s argument for ending the war competes with the position of advisers who defend military pressure. That gives voters a difference to judge; it does not establish that support has already moved from one candidate to another.

relationships.kind: Wiles would leave the chief-of-staff job to Miller
relationships.assessment: The reported handover would give Miller the White House staff role Wiles currently holds. Her continued political influence depends on what responsibilities she actually receives outside that job.

relationships.kind: Investors and fundraisers with past links to Vance
relationships.assessment: Past financial backing and fundraising relationships could help Vance recruit money and staff. They do not establish agreement with him on every policy or a new commitment to a presidential campaign.

power_shifts.role_change: Wiles is expected to leave the White House chief-of-staff job for Trump’s political team.
power_shifts.implication: As chief of staff, Wiles can influence which people and proposals reach Trump. Leaving that job would give her less control over day-to-day White House decisions. She may still advise Trump about elections, but her new responsibilities and any authority over campaign money are not yet confirmed.

power_shifts.role_change: Miller is expected to take over as White House chief of staff.
power_shifts.implication: Miller would gain more influence over the officials, staffing choices and policy proposals presented to Trump. That could help him push stricter immigration enforcement. The appointment itself does not order a policy change or show that he will win every argument about Iran.

power_method.title: How the access ratings work
power_method.scale: The scale compares jobs, not measured shares of political power: 0 means no identified way to influence the decision; 1 means an outside adviser; 2 means a role in Trump’s political team; 3 means a deputy White House role; 4 means the chief of staff; 5 means the president, who makes the final executive decision.
power_method.status: These are estimates of how much access each job could provide to Trump after the reported handover. They do not mean that either adviser controls a percentage of the administration.
power_method.condition: This comparison assumes that the reported November 9 handover happens and that Wiles moves to Trump’s political team. Both advisers’ actual responsibilities still need confirmation.
power_method.policy_projection: Miller could use the chief-of-staff job to prioritize immigration enforcement and staff who favor it. That does not establish that the Iran war will escalate: the record also includes reporting that Miller argued for an exit. Incoming Democratic majorities could demand records and challenge funding once the new Congress begins.
